Chapter 3: The Problems with Central Banking and Fiat Money
Think about this for a second—when was the last time you held a gold coin, or even saw one in person?
Most of us don’t deal with gold or silver anymore. Instead, we’re used to numbers on a screen, plastic cards, and quick taps on our phones.
But behind all that convenience, there’s a hidden world where central banks make big decisions. They set interest rates, print money, and try to guide the economy. For most people, this is just how things work—it feels normal, maybe even unchangeable.
But here’s the thing: the whole system is sitting on a pretty fragile foundation.
Picture a family working hard to save for their kids’ education. Month after month, they put money aside, hoping those savings will grow. But as the years go by, tuition keeps climbing, and their savings just can’t keep up.
It’s not just bad luck. It’s inflation—the quiet force that chips away at what you’ve earned. See, when central banks create more money, every dollar or euro you hold loses a bit of its value.
Prices go up, and suddenly your savings don’t buy as much as you thought they would.
Most people don’t see the full picture. Sure, they notice their weekly grocery bill going up, but not many connect it to decisions made in distant, closed-door meetings. Central banks often say a little bit of inflation is actually good—it keeps people spending and keeps the economy moving.
But if you’re trying to save, it can feel like running on a treadmill that just keeps speeding up.
The power to create money isn’t just about economics—it’s also about control. Governments can fund wars, bail out banks, or launch huge projects without ever raising taxes. They just borrow or print more money.
In the moment, it can smooth out a crisis. But over time, it builds up debt and throws the economy off balance.
And what happens then? Financial crises start popping up more often. Banks feel safe taking bigger risks, knowing there’s likely a safety net if things go wrong. Asset bubbles swell and then suddenly burst, and it’s everyday people who end up paying the price.
The connection between hard work and fair reward gets weaker, and trust in the whole system starts to fade.
Some people try to break free by investing in real estate, stocks, or whatever assets they can find. But those markets? They’re shaped by central bank policies, too. When interest rates are low, asset prices can shoot up, making it even harder for folks just starting out to get ahead.
The gap between people who already have assets and those who don’t just keeps getting wider.
The story of fiat money—the kind created just because a government says so—shows how easy it is to forget what gives money real value. When money isn’t tied to something scarce, it turns into a tool for quick fixes and political promises.
Instead of being disciplined about spending, it’s all too tempting to kick the can down the road and hope for the best later.
For a lot of people, it feels like the system is rigged. You work hard, you save, you try your best—but the rules always seem to shift.
So, the search for something better—a kind of money that can’t be inflated or manipulated—starts to feel urgent.
The stage is set for a whole new approach, one that learns from the past but also takes advantage of the technology we have today.
